items.prompt: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly.
items.sentence: Our two ___ hutch needs fresh straw before the cold nights.
items.hint: There are two owners, so the apostrophe goes after the plural s.
items.explanation: When something belongs to more than one owner, write the plural word first and add the apostrophe after the s: rabbits' hutch.

items.prompt: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly.
items.sentence: The ___ guitar case was covered in shiny stickers.
items.hint: One performer owns the case, so add an apostrophe then s.
items.explanation: One busker owns the guitar case, so we write busker's: the apostrophe comes before the s for a single owner.

items.prompt: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly.
items.sentence: The ___ artwork hung proudly in the front office.
items.hint: Children is already plural, so treat it like a single owning word.
items.explanation: Children is a special plural that does not end in s, so we show ownership by adding apostrophe then s: children's.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
options: Our ponys saddle needs a good clean.
Our pony's saddle needs a good clean.
Our ponys' saddle needs a good clean.
Our pony saddle's needs a good clean.
items.hint: One pony owns the saddle, so where should the apostrophe sit?
items.explanation: The saddle belongs to one pony, so we write pony's saddle with the apostrophe before the s.

items.prompt: Choose the preposition that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The ferry chugged slowly ___ the harbour towards the wharf.
items.hint: Picture the ferry travelling from one side of the water to the other.
items.explanation: Across describes movement from one side of the harbour to the other, which matches how a ferry travels.

items.prompt: Choose the preposition that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: We sheltered ___ the rock ledge until the shower passed.
items.hint: To stay dry, you need the ledge above your head.
items.explanation: Under shows position below something. The ledge is overhead, keeping the rain off.

items.prompt: Choose the preposition that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The lorikeets squabbled ___ the branches of the flowering gum.
items.hint: Which word means surrounded by or in the middle of many things?
items.explanation: Among means in the middle of several things. The birds are surrounded by many branches.

items.prompt: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: ___ we laced up our boots and hit the trail.
items.hint: A phrase at the front of a sentence needs a comma after it.
items.explanation: When a sentence opens with a phrase like After breakfast, a comma separates it from the main part of the sentence.

items.prompt: Which sentence has the comma in the correct place?
options: During, the science lesson our volcano model fizzed everywhere.
During the science, lesson our volcano model fizzed everywhere.
During the science lesson our volcano model, fizzed everywhere.
During the science lesson, our volcano model fizzed everywhere.
items.hint: Find where the opening phrase ends and the main action begins.
items.explanation: The fronted phrase is During the science lesson, so the comma belongs straight after it, before the main clause.

items.prompt: Which sentence has the comma in the correct place?
options: Before the concert, we tuned our ukuleles backstage.
Before the concert we, tuned our ukuleles backstage.
Before, the concert we tuned our ukuleles backstage.
Before the, concert we tuned our ukuleles backstage.
items.hint: The whole opening phrase tells us when, and the comma comes after all of it.
items.explanation: Before the concert is the fronted phrase, so the comma sits at the end of it, just before we.

items.prompt: Which sentence punctuates the direct speech correctly?
options: "There's a starfish in this rock pool"! shouted Mia.
"There's a starfish in this rock pool!" shouted Mia.
"There's a starfish in this rock pool!" Shouted Mia.
There's a starfish in this rock pool!" shouted Mia.
items.hint: The exclamation mark stays inside the quotation marks, and the next word stays lowercase.
items.explanation: Punctuation for the spoken words sits inside the closing quotation marks, and shouted does not start a new sentence, so it stays lowercase.

items.prompt: Which sentence punctuates the direct speech correctly?
options: Dad said "Hold the torch steady while I fix the tyre."
Dad said, "hold the torch steady while I fix the tyre."
Dad said, "Hold the torch steady while I fix the tyre."
Dad said, "Hold the torch steady while I fix the tyre".
items.hint: You need a comma before the speech, a capital to start it, and the full stop inside the quotes.
items.explanation: A comma follows the speaker, the spoken words begin with a capital letter, and the full stop belongs inside the closing quotation marks.

items.prompt: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly.
items.sentence: "The tide is coming in fast," ___ the lifeguard.
items.hint: The words after the speech carry on the same sentence, so no capital and no extra punctuation.
items.explanation: The reporting words carry on the same sentence after the speech, so warned stays lowercase with no extra comma or full stop.

items.prompt: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly.
items.sentence: Mrs Chen announced, "___ robotics club starts at lunchtime today."
items.hint: Spoken words always begin like a brand-new sentence.
items.explanation: Direct speech starts with a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence, so The is correct.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: That was the ___ wave I have ever surfed.
items.hint: Comparing with everything ever means you need the superlative form.
items.explanation: Ever tells us we are comparing against all waves, so we need the superlative biggest, with no extra most.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: My banana bread rose ___ than the loaf I baked last week.
items.hint: The word than is a clue that you are comparing just two things.
items.explanation: Than signals a comparison between two things, so we use the comparative higher, never more higher.

items.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
options: This is the most tastiest pizza we have ever made.
This is the tastiest pizza we have ever made.
This is the tastier pizza we have ever made.
This is the most tastier pizza we have ever made.
items.hint: Never double up most with an -est or -er ending.
items.explanation: Tastiest already shows the highest level, so adding most is doubling up. Tastier compares only two things.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The guinea pig twitched ___ nose at the slice of capsicum.
items.hint: Try swapping in it is - if the sentence breaks, you need the ownership word.
items.explanation: Its without an apostrophe shows belonging. It's always means it is, which would not make sense here.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The hikers checked the ___ forecast before starting the steep climb.
items.hint: You need the word about rain, wind and sunshine.
items.explanation: Weather means the conditions outside, like rain or sunshine. Whether introduces a choice between options.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Please put the kayak paddles over ___ by the shed.
items.hint: You need the word that points to a place.
items.explanation: There tells us about a place. Their shows belonging, and they're is short for they are.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The echidna, ___ was digging near the track, ignored us completely.
items.hint: Choose the relative pronoun we use for animals and things.
items.explanation: Which introduces extra information about animals and things. Who is kept for people.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The neighbour ___ owns the blue heeler waved to us from the verandah.
items.hint: You need the relative pronoun for a person doing the action.
items.explanation: Who refers to a person doing something. The neighbour owns the dog, so who is correct.

items.prompt: Which of these is a complete sentence?
options: When the whistle blew, the relay began.
Because the tide was too low for the boat.
Although we trained hard all season.
The oval that we mowed yesterday.
items.hint: A complete sentence needs a main clause that can stand on its own.
items.explanation: Only one option has a main clause: the relay began. The others are fragments that leave you waiting for more.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: A gust of wind had ___ our map into the creek.
items.hint: After the helper had, use the special past form of blow.
items.explanation: With the helping verb had, we need the past participle blown. Blew stands alone without a helper.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: By sunrise the puddles on the driveway had ___ solid.
items.hint: The helper had needs the participle form, not the plain past tense.
items.explanation: Freeze is irregular: froze works alone, but after had we need frozen. Freezed is never a word.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Ivy has ___ her own comic strip for the school newsletter.
items.hint: Which form of draw follows the helper has?
items.explanation: After has, the irregular verb draw becomes drawn. Drew only works on its own, as in she drew it yesterday.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Last summer we ___ across the lake to the pontoon.
items.hint: There is no helping verb here, so use the simple past form.
items.explanation: Without a helper like have, the simple past swam is correct. Swum only follows a helping verb, as in have swum.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly to add extra information?
options: Uncle Theo, who grows amazing tomatoes gave us a whole box.
Uncle Theo who grows amazing tomatoes, gave us a whole box.
Uncle Theo, who grows amazing tomatoes, gave us a whole box.
Uncle Theo who, grows amazing tomatoes, gave us a whole box.
items.hint: Extra information needs a comma at both ends, like a pair of brackets.
items.explanation: The clause who grows amazing tomatoes is extra information, so it needs a comma before and after it.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly to add extra information?
options: The old jetty weathered and grey, is the best fishing spot in town.
The old jetty, weathered and grey is the best fishing spot in town.
The old jetty, weathered, and grey, is the best fishing spot in town.
The old jetty, weathered and grey, is the best fishing spot in town.
items.hint: Try lifting the describing phrase out - the sentence should still make sense.
items.explanation: Weathered and grey is extra description, so a comma goes on each side of the whole phrase. If you remove it, the sentence still works.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly to add extra information?
options: Our librarian, who loves detective stories, recommended a mystery novel.
Our librarian, who loves detective stories recommended a mystery novel.
Our librarian who loves detective stories, recommended a mystery novel.
Our librarian who, loves detective stories, recommended a mystery novel.
items.hint: Extra information dropped into a sentence needs a comma at both ends, like a pair of brackets.
items.explanation: The clause who loves detective stories is extra information, so it is wrapped in a pair of commas, one before and one after. A single comma leaves the pair unfinished.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The list of camping supplies ___ pinned to the fridge.
items.hint: Find the real subject - is it the list or the supplies?
items.explanation: The subject is the list, which is singular, so it takes is. Of camping supplies just adds detail.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: One of the emus at the sanctuary ___ escaped into the car park.
items.hint: The subject is one, not the whole group of birds.
items.explanation: One is the singular subject, so it takes has. The phrase of the emus does not change the verb.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Maths ___ my favourite subject because I love solving puzzles.
items.hint: Some words end in s but still name one single thing.
items.explanation: Maths ends in s but names one subject, so it is singular and takes is.

items.prompt: Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Neither the twins nor their cousin ___ ever tried rock climbing.
items.hint: With nor, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.
items.explanation: After neither-nor, the verb matches the nearer subject. Cousin is singular, so has is correct.

items.prompt: Which sentence makes it completely clear who was carrying the beach umbrella?
options: When Talia met her sister, she was carrying a beach umbrella.
Talia was carrying a beach umbrella when she met her sister.
When Talia met her sister, she had it with her.
She was carrying a beach umbrella when Talia met her sister.
items.hint: Check whether each pronoun can only point to one person.
items.explanation: Naming Talia as the carrier before any pronoun appears removes the confusion. In the other options, she could mean either person.

items.prompt: Choose the option that makes it completely clear who boarded the ferry.
items.sentence: Asha waved to Chloe as ___ boarded the ferry.
items.hint: A pronoun here could point to either girl - what removes the doubt?
items.explanation: Using the name Chloe makes the meaning certain. The pronoun she could refer to either Asha or Chloe, and her and herself cannot act as the subject.

items.prompt: Which sentence makes it completely clear who scored the winning goal?
options: Marco passed to Denny and he scored the winning goal.
Marco passed to Denny, who scored the winning goal.
Marco passed to him and he scored the winning goal.
He passed to him and scored the winning goal.
items.hint: Look for the option where the scoring is tied directly to one player.
items.explanation: Who sits right next to Denny, so it can only mean Denny scored. The pronoun he could point to either player.

items.prompt: Choose the word that correctly joins the two ideas into one sentence.
items.sentence: We missed the bus, ___ we jogged all the way to training.
items.hint: The second idea is the result of the first.
items.explanation: So shows a result: missing the bus caused the jog. A comma alone would leave a run-on sentence.

items.prompt: Which option fixes the run-on sentence 'The thunder rumbled we ran for the tent'?
options: The thunder rumbled, we ran for the tent.
The thunder rumbled we ran, for the tent.
The thunder, rumbled we ran for the tent.
The thunder rumbled, so we ran for the tent.
items.hint: A comma on its own cannot glue two complete ideas together.
items.explanation: Two complete ideas need a joining word like so, not just a comma. A comma alone creates a comma splice.

items.prompt: Which option fixes the run-on sentence correctly?
options: My cousin loves astronomy. She saved up for a telescope.
My cousin loves astronomy, she saved up for a telescope.
My cousin loves astronomy she saved up for a telescope.
My cousin loves astronomy, saved up for a telescope.
items.hint: Two complete ideas can each stand alone as separate sentences.
items.explanation: Splitting the run-on into two full sentences with a full stop and a capital letter fixes it. A comma alone is not strong enough.
